newsitem.title: FRANCE: UNESCO enthusiastic about Britain's return.
newsitem.headline: UNESCO enthusiastic about Britain's return.

text.p: UNESCO enthusiastically welcomed on Wednesday the British Labour government's decision to rejoin the organisation 12 years after the Conservatives slammed the door.

"I enthusiastically welcome the United Kingdom's decision to rejoin UNESCO, an organisation it has played so central a role in founding and helping define its mission," UNESCO Director-General Federico Mayor said in a statement.
Queen Elizabeth officially announced at the opening of the new Labour-dominated parliament that Britain was returning to the United Nations Educational Scientific and Cultural Organisation.

Mayor recalled that UNESCO's constitution was adopted in Westminster in 1945 and said he looked forward to British educators, scientists, intellectuals and artists contributing to UNESCO's mission of building peace founded upon freedom and justice.
"In promoting principles of democracy and universal ethical values, the role of the United Kingdom is particularly important," Mayor said.
Foreign Minister Robin Cook had said Britain would rejoin during a ministerial meeting of the Western European Union (WEU) held at UNESCO's Paris headquarters on Tuesday.
President Ronald Reagan took the United States out of UNESCO in 1984 and Britain's Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher followed suit the following year.
Between them the two countries, accusing UNESCO of poor management and anti-Western bias, took away 30 percent of its budget.

Spain's Mayor took over from Senegal's Amadou Mahtar M'Bow in 1987 and embarked on cutting bloated bureaucracy and improved management of the agency which strives to promote education and respect of human rights as well as scientific and cultural exchanges.

President Bill Clinton has said rejoining UNESCO is a priority for his administration if the necessary dues can be coaxed out of a reluctant Congress. The United States needs $65 million a year in dues to regain full membership.
